A memory circuit layout design includes four abutting memory cell regions, each corresponding to a respective memory cell. These memory cell regions are arranged adjacent to one another so that the cells share common layout boundaries within the overall memory circuit.

The layout further includes a first oxide diffusion layout pattern associated with the first and second memory cells. This first oxide diffusion layout pattern defines active diffusion regions used to form the first and second memory cells and includes a shared source portion. The shared source portion overlaps the memory cell regions of both the first and second memory cells, thereby providing a common source region for those two cells.

A second oxide diffusion layout pattern is provided for the third and fourth memory cells. Similar to the first oxide diffusion layout pattern, the second oxide diffusion layout pattern defines active diffusion regions used to form the third and fourth memory cells. The second oxide diffusion layout pattern also includes a shared source portion that overlaps the memory cell regions of both the third and fourth memory cells, thereby forming a common source region shared by the third and fourth memory cells.

The memory circuit layout design also includes a first conductive layout pattern. This first conductive layout pattern extends in a second direction across the layout and overlaps the shared source portions of both the first oxide diffusion layout pattern and the second oxide diffusion layout pattern. In this manner, the first conductive layout pattern may electrically connect or otherwise interface with the shared source portions associated with the first and second memory cells and with the third and fourth memory cells.
outputs.L4:
A memory circuit layout design is provided in which a plurality of memory cell regions are arranged adjacent to one another in an abutting configuration. In one example, the layout includes four memory cell regions positioned so that neighboring memory cells share common boundary areas. Each memory cell region may contain transistor structures, diffusion regions, gate structures, source regions, drain regions, and associated interconnection features used to form the memory circuit.

The layout includes oxide diffusion patterns that are shared between paired memory cells. In particular, a first oxide diffusion pattern may be arranged across a boundary between a first memory cell region and a second memory cell region, while a second oxide diffusion pattern may be arranged across a boundary between a third memory cell region and a fourth memory cell region. These shared oxide diffusion patterns define common active regions that can be used by adjacent cells, allowing the paired memory cells to share source portions rather than requiring each cell to include a separate isolated source region.

A conductive pattern is further provided over or coupled to the shared source portions of the oxide diffusion patterns. The conductive pattern extends across the shared source areas and electrically connects the source regions of the paired memory cells. This conductive pattern may be formed using a metal layer, a local interconnect layer, a contact structure, or another suitable conductive material. By extending across the shared source portions, the conductive pattern provides a common source connection for adjacent memory cells and supports efficient routing of source lines within the memory array.

The arrangement of the four abutting memory cell regions allows the memory cells to be placed closer together while maintaining the necessary electrical connections. Because adjacent cells share oxide diffusion regions and source structures, the layout reduces redundant diffusion areas and decreases the amount of space required for isolation and separate source contacts. This improves the overall area efficiency of the memory circuit and can increase memory density within a semiconductor device.

In addition, the shared source configuration helps organize interconnections in the memory circuit. Instead of routing separate conductive lines to individual source regions for each memory cell, a common conductive pattern can be used to connect multiple shared source portions. This simplifies the layout, reduces routing congestion, and may improve manufacturability by providing a more regular and repeatable cell arrangement.

Accordingly, the described memory circuit layout provides a compact and efficient structure for arranging adjacent memory cells. By using abutting memory cell regions, shared oxide diffusion patterns, and conductive patterns extending across shared source portions, the layout enables shared source structures between neighboring memory cells. This configuration supports improved integration density, reduced layout area, and more organized electrical interconnection within the memory circuit.
outputs.L5:
A memory circuit is an electronic circuit designed to store information in the form of electrical signals. It is an essential part of many digital systems, including computers, smartphones, microcontrollers, and embedded devices. The main purpose of a memory circuit is to hold data so that it can be accessed, processed, or changed when needed.

Memory circuits can be built using different components, such as flip-flops, capacitors, transistors, or magnetic elements. In digital electronics, a basic memory circuit often stores one bit of data, either a 0 or a 1. By combining many memory cells together, larger amounts of information can be stored.

There are several types of memory circuits. RAM, or Random Access Memory, temporarily stores data while a device is operating. ROM, or Read-Only Memory, stores permanent instructions that are not easily changed. Other types, such as flash memory, can keep data even when the power is turned off.

A simple memory circuit may use a latch or a flip-flop. These circuits can maintain their output state until they receive a signal to change it. This ability to “remember” a previous state makes them useful in counters, registers, processors, and control systems.

In modern technology, memory circuits are extremely important because they allow electronic devices to store programs, save user data, and perform complex tasks quickly. Without memory circuits, digital systems would not be able to function efficiently or retain information.
